title: Insulation Resistance Testing with a Megger: Step by Step
text:
Electrical Safety & Standards

 Insulation Resistance Testing with a Megger: Step by Step

 A motor that trips on startup after sitting idle for months is usually telling you its insulation absorbed moisture, and Insulation Resistance Testing with a megger is how you confirm that before reenergizing anything.

 
 Insulation Resistance Testing 
 Megger 
 Polarization Index 
 IEEE 43 
 




 Insulation Resistance Testing with a megger applies a DC voltage across a conductor's insulation and measures the leakage current, giving a megohm reading that shows whether the insulation is dry and sound or contaminated and failing.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to walk through Insulation Resistance Testing with a megger step by step, the correct test voltage for different equipment, how to read the result, and the mistakes that ruin an otherwise good test.


 This is worth doing before any earthing work too, since a Single Line Diagram showing every isolation point makes it far easier to identify exactly what needs to be deenergized first.


 
 
 
 Insulation Resistance Testing


 Insulation Resistance Testing, often shortened to IR testing, works by applying a steady DC voltage between a conductor and earth, or between two conductors, then measuring the tiny leakage current that flows through the insulation to calculate resistance in megohms.


 Good insulation blocks nearly all of that current, giving a high megohm reading, while damp, dirty, or degraded insulation lets more current leak through, giving a lower reading that gets worse as the problem progresses.


 The megger itself is simply a hand cranked or battery powered device that generates the test DC voltage and reads the resulting current directly in megohms, no separate voltmeter or ammeter is ever needed to correctly interpret the display.

 IR Testing Step by Step


 
 1
 Isolate and deenergize the circuit or equipment completely, then lock out and tag the isolation point before touching anything.


 2
 Discharge any stored energy in cables or capacitors by briefly grounding the conductor before connecting test leads.


 3
 Disconnect sensitive electronic devices, drives, and control circuits, since test voltage can permanently damage their internal components.


 4
 Select the correct test voltage on the megger based on the equipment's rated operating voltage.


 5
 Connect the line lead to the conductor under test and the earth lead to ground or the equipment frame.


 6
 Apply the test, hold for the full duration, and record the reading at exactly one minute and again at ten minutes if checking polarization index.


 7
 Discharge the conductor again after the test completes, then record the result before restoring the circuit.





 Skipping step two is the single most common way to damage a megger or give an inexperienced technician a nasty shock, cables and motor windings hold a genuine charge after testing and after being deenergized.


 Why the Discharge Steps Matter


 Long cables and motor windings behave like capacitors, storing charge from the test voltage itself. That stored energy has nowhere to go once the megger disconnects, so the conductor stays live at a dangerous voltage until something drains it away.


 A dedicated discharge resistor built into most modern meggers handles this automatically at the end of a test cycle, but older or basic units may need a manual shorting stick applied by someone who knows exactly what they are doing.


 Never assume a device has fully discharged just because the meter dropped to zero, a truly safe conductor should also be verified with a separate voltage tester before bare hands or tools touch it directly, every single time.


 Recording a Baseline


 The very first IR test on a new piece of equipment is worth recording carefully as a baseline, since every future reading gets compared against it rather than against a generic industry number.


 A motor that reads 200 megohms new and drops to 20 megohms two years later has lost 90 percent of its insulation quality, even though 20 megohms alone might still look perfectly acceptable against a simple pass or fail chart.


 Logging that baseline in the same maintenance record used for vibration or thermal readings keeps insulation trending visible alongside every other health indicator already tracked for that same piece of asset.


 Selecting the Correct Test Voltage


 
 
 Equipment Rating Recommended Test Voltage 

 Up to 500V 500V DC 

 500V to 1000V 1000V DC 

 Above 1000V 2500V DC or higher 

 



 
 
 Advertisement 


 
 


 Interpreting the Reading


 
 IEEE 43 Minimum
 Rated voltage in kilovolts plus one, expressed as a minimum acceptable megohm value


 Good Reading
 Above 5 megohms is generally considered healthy for low voltage motors and cables


 Polarization Index
 Ten minute reading divided by one minute reading, above 2 is typically acceptable


 Dielectric Absorption Ratio
 Sixty second reading divided by thirty second reading, above 1.4 suggests dry insulation





 
 Did You Know

 A single megohm reading only tells you the insulation's condition at that moment, trending the same test over months or years reveals gradual insulation degradation long before a single low reading would raise alarm.




 Temperature Correction


 Insulation resistance readings drop as winding temperature rises, roughly halving for every ten degree Celsius increase above the reference temperature the manufacturer used when publishing minimum values.


 A hot motor tested right after shutdown can read misleadingly low even with perfectly healthy insulation, so either let equipment cool to a standard reference temperature first or apply a correction factor before comparing the reading against a minimum value.
